t: Mongolian is the principal Mongolic language; its written history begins in the 13th century, when Genghis Khan adopted a script from the Uyghurs and the Mongol Empire spoke Middle Mongol.
Its vowels follow strict harmony and its grammar builds words from chains of suffixes, with seven to nine cases and five voices.

Written in more scripts than almost any other language, it is spoken today by perhaps 5–6 million people, in Cyrillic in Mongolia and in the traditional script in Inner Mongolia, where since 2023 Mandarin has been the only language of instruction in its schools.
dyk: The Cyrillic script, closer to the spoken language than the traditional one, helped raise literacy in Mongolia from 17.3% to 73.5% between 1941 and 1950; campaigns using the traditional script had raised it only from 3.0% to 17.3% between 1921 and 1940.
ev: Genghis Khan adopts a script for the Mongolian language, adapted from the Uyghur alphabet
The Stele of Yisüngge, perhaps the earliest surviving Mongolian text, records a report on sports in stone
Middle Mongol is written in four scripts: Uyghur Mongolian, ’Phags-pa for decrees, Chinese for The Secret History of the Mongols, and Arabic for dictionaries
Classical Mongolian, a highly standardised written language, begins; its great works include the Mongolian Kangyur and Tengyur
The Soyombo alphabet is created for Buddhist texts
Cyrillic is made mandatory in the Mongolian state, after a Latin alphabet adopted that year lasts two months
An attempt to bring back the traditional script in Mongolia fails in the face of popular resistance
China requires three subjects to be taught in Mandarin in Inner Mongolia’s Mongolian-language schools; the protests that follow are quickly suppressed

f.family: Mongolic: the principal language of the family, in its Common (Central) Mongolic branch, and related to the extinct Khitan; the old Altaic grouping with Turkic, Tungusic, Korean and Japonic is now seen as obsolete by most comparative linguists.
f.script: The traditional Mongolian script, adapted from the Uyghur script and adopted by Genghis Khan in 1204; also ’Phags-pa, Chinese characters and Arabic in the 13th–15th centuries, Soyombo (1686) and the Clear Script of the Oirats; in Mongolia Cyrillic, mandatory from 1941.
f.earliest: The Stele of Yisüngge, most often dated 1224 or 1225, may be the earliest surviving Mongolian text; Kirakos of Gandzak’s 13th-century Mongolian-Armenian list of 55 words is the first manuscript evidence. The Bugut (584) and Hüis Tolgoi (604–620) inscriptions are older Mongolic or Para-Mongolic texts.
f.status: Living: perhaps 5–6 million speakers across its dialects, nearly 3.6 million in Mongolia (2014 estimate) and about 2.1 million in Inner Mongolia; the official language of Mongolia and of Inner Mongolia, and recognised in Xinjiang, Qinghai and Buryatia.
